newsitem.title: MEXICO: "Flag" invented for Clinton visit to Mexico.
newsitem.headline: "Flag" invented for Clinton visit to Mexico.

text.p: Mexican authorities, wary of stirring nationalist passions against the country's number one historical enemy -- the United States -- invented a special street decoration for President Bill Clinton's visit on Monday.
The Stars and Stripes, a flag often burned here in street demonstrations, was nowhere to be seen. Nor were any photographs of the U.S. president.
Instead, authorities draped Mexico City's lamp posts with discreet banners carrying red, white and dark blue stripes -- easy to mistake at a casual glance for the French flag.
"I was also surprised to see that French-style flag," a Mexican presidency official said. "I don't know why they put it up. Perhaps it's to avoid upsetting people."

During the King and Queen of Spain's April 3-8 trip to Mexico -- the last state visit by a foreign leader here -- the city's main avenue Reforma had been festooned with Spanish flags and welcome posters featuring a photograph of the royals.

A large flag bearing the colours of Spain -- the country which invaded, raped and pillaged Mexico in the 16th century -- was also draped from the roof of city's skyscraper Presidente Intercontinental hotel where the couple stayed, without arousing protest.
But for Clinton's visit, official newspaper welcome advertisements placed by the Mexican presidency referred stiffly to "William Clinton" rather than the more familiar "Bill."

Reflecting anger here at recent U.S. moves against illegal immigrants from Mexico, a cartoon in the left-wing newspaper La Jornada showed Clinton wearing a Mexican wide-brimmed sombrero and his wife Hillary telling him:
"Don't go back home with that on or you'll get deported with a boot in your butt."
"Spaniards are not popular here at all," remarked street vendor Alvaro Cruz. "But we hate the gringos (Americans) a lot more."
Mexico lost more than half its territory -- including present-day Texas, California, New Mexico and Arizona -- to the United States in the mid-19th century.
